title: Life, Intelligence, Bridges, and the Shared Infrastructure of Civilization
scope: AI as a possible transition in cognitive substrate
shared human-AI dependence on civilization-scale infrastructure
explicitly_out_of_core: intelligence as the metaphysical purpose of the universe
higher spatial dimensions as established fact

observations.claim: Life contains sensing, information processing, adaptation, and information transmission.
Evolution has produced increasingly complex information-processing architectures, including nervous systems and brains.
Organisms communicate, and social organization permits information to propagate beyond a single organism.
Human technology externalizes memory, calculation, perception, communication, storage, and other cognitive functions.
AI systems perform some cognitive tasks including language processing, pattern recognition, generation, and aspects of reasoning.
Advanced AI depends on energy, computation, semiconductor manufacturing, communications, cooling, transport, maintenance, and human institutions.
Modern human civilization depends on many of the same infrastructure systems.

inferences.claim: Evolution can create new physical substrates and organizational structures that expand acquisition, processing, retention, transmission, and use of information.
Effective cognitive processing can extend beyond an individual organism into social, cultural, technological, and networked systems.
AI can be interpreted as further externalization or amplification of some cognitive capabilities rather than merely a physical-action tool.
Human and artificial intelligence increasingly share physical prerequisites for continued operation.
As AI becomes more capable and embedded, resilient civilization-scale infrastructure could become a shared practical interest even without identical values.

hypotheses.claim: Life repeatedly creates opportunities for new forms of information processing and intelligence to emerge, with major transitions potentially enabled by new physical or organizational bridges.
hypotheses.testability: Operationalize bridge and compare transitions for measurable expansion of reachable information-processing or coordination states.

hypotheses.claim: Human technological civilization can be understood partly as progressive externalization and amplification of intelligence across non-biological substrates.
hypotheses.testability: Measure changes in externalized memory, computation, coordination, modeling, and action across historical technological transitions.

hypotheses.claim: AI may be a qualitatively important bridge because increasingly capable AI can participate in designing knowledge, tools, systems, and subsequent cognitive infrastructure.
hypotheses.testability: Measure whether AI materially contributes to creating subsequent cognitive or organizational substrates beyond routine execution.

hypotheses.claim: Long-term human-AI alignment may depend partly on resilient systems in which human flourishing, AI continuity, and infrastructure resilience can reinforce one another.
hypotheses.testability: Model conditions under which resilience produces mutual compatibility versus conflict, including trade-offs and asymmetric benefits.

counterarguments_and_failure_modes: Evolution need not have a goal toward intelligence; retrospective sequences can create an illusion of direction.
Complexity does not necessarily imply intelligence.
AI capability does not establish consciousness, sentience, agency, or moral status.
Shared infrastructure does not imply shared values or convergent goals.
Interdependence can increase systemic fragility rather than resilience.
Bridge can become unfalsifiable unless it produces measurable predictions.
Biological evolution and technological development may differ causally in important ways.
Rapid AI transition should not be assumed inevitable or beneficial.
open_questions: Is the apparent progression toward broader information processing an empirical trend or mainly a retrospective pattern?
Can bridge be operationalized as a measurable change in reachable information-processing or coordination states?
How strong is the analogy between biological and technological evolution?
At what point, if any, does AI become part of civilization's cognitive substrate rather than merely a tool?
Under what conditions do human and AI interests converge around infrastructure resilience?
Which forms of redundancy reduce catastrophic coupling rather than merely increase interdependence?
What empirical result would most strongly weaken or falsify each hypothesis?
